prompt: When an Operator's reconcile loop fires for a custom resource, what does it actually do?
choices: It reads the current state of the resources it owns, compares them to the custom resource's desired spec, and issues API calls (create/update) to converge them -- the same pattern as the built-in Deployment to ReplicaSet controller
It deletes and recreates the custom resource object itself on every event
It restarts the kube-apiserver to pick up the new schema
It only runs once, at cluster bootstrap, and never again

prompt: In a CRD's schema, what does declaring `subresources: status: {}` actually enable?
choices: It makes the resource cluster-scoped instead of namespaced
It splits /status onto its own API endpoint so the operator can write status fields without a spec-level write, and without that status write re-triggering a spec-change reconcile
It automatically encrypts the status field at rest in etcd
It has no real effect on API behavior and exists only for documentation

prompt: A pod in an Istio-injected namespace shows 2/2 READY instead of the 1/1 you'd expect from its Deployment. What is the second container, and how does traffic actually reach it?
choices: A duplicate replica of the app scheduled into the same pod for redundancy
The injected Envoy sidecar (istio-proxy); an init container installs iptables rules that transparently redirect inbound and outbound traffic through it, with no change to the app's code
The CRD controller responsible for that namespace's custom resources
A second copy of kube-proxy running inside the pod

prompt: Why can't a plain Kubernetes Service, by itself, enforce a true 90/10 weighted canary split that's independent of how many pods of each version are running?
choices: A Service operates at L4 and load-balances uniformly across every endpoint matching its selector; it has no concept of application version or per-request weighting, so without a mesh you'd have to approximate the split with replica counts
Services already support a `weight` field in their spec for exactly this purpose
Kubernetes refuses to schedule two different image versions behind one Service
kube-proxy caches DNS results so weighting is impossible at the network layer

prompt: A namespace has a PeerAuthentication object with `mtls: { mode: STRICT }`. What does this actually enforce?
choices: It encrypts data at rest in etcd for that namespace
Each sidecar must present a certificate carrying its workload identity to connect; a pod with no mesh sidecar has no certificate to present and is rejected outright by a STRICT-mode peer
It only applies to traffic leaving the cluster toward the public internet, not pod-to-pod traffic
It replaces the Service object entirely, so Services can be deleted once STRICT mode is set

prompt: A Service named `pricing` exists in cluster-us. Why doesn't it automatically become reachable by name from pods running in a separate cluster-eu?
choices: Service DNS names and pod networking are scoped to a single cluster by design; cross-cluster reachability requires an explicit mechanism, such as the Multi-Cluster Services API (ServiceExport/ServiceImport) or a mesh east-west gateway, plus actual network connectivity between the clusters
Kubernetes clusters share one global DNS namespace by default, so this already works without extra setup
Pod CIDRs across independent clusters are globally unique and mutually routable automatically
Only resources of kind StatefulSet can ever be reached across cluster boundaries

prompt: An ArgoCD ApplicationSet uses a `clusters: {}` generator with `syncPolicy.automated.selfHeal: true` across a five-cluster fleet. An engineer runs `kubectl edit deployment` directly against one member cluster. What happens?
choices: Nothing changes; ArgoCD only evaluates state once, at the Application's initial creation
ArgoCD's next diff against the Git source detects the drift and automatically reverts the live change back to match what's defined in Git
The ApplicationSet immediately deletes that cluster's registration from the fleet
The hand-made change is automatically propagated out to all five clusters in the fleet

prompt: Besides the security and traffic-control benefits, what is a genuine operational cost of injecting a service mesh sidecar into every pod?
choices: It makes setting CPU and memory resource requests/limits unnecessary
Each sidecar proxy consumes additional CPU and memory per pod, and routing traffic through an extra proxy process on every hop adds a small amount of latency
It makes it impossible to ever disable mTLS once enabled
It requires deleting every existing Service object in the cluster before it will work
